\subsection{Conditional Decomposition of LP Selection}\label{app:conditional_decomp}

To test whether the two-factor pattern holds within datasets, we restrict LP selection to the favorable subset: non-degenerate instances whose within-instance LP range exceeds the dataset-specific median (SciERC: 0.040 nats, CoNLL: 0.062, Few-NERD: 0.067).
Table~\ref{tab:conditional_decomp} reports results across three datasets.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{LP selection on the favorable subset (non-degenerate instances with LP range above the dataset-specific median) per dataset (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). CI: bootstrap 95\% confidence interval.}
\label{tab:conditional_decomp}
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
Dataset & LP $\Delta$ (pp) & 95\% CI & Interpretation \\
\midrule
SciERC & $+$2.47 & [$+$0.30, $+$4.70] & significant positive \\
Few-NERD & $+$0.63 & [$-$0.02, $+$1.30] & marginal positive \\
CoNLL & $-$1.78 & [$-$2.83, $-$0.76] & significant negative \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The two-factor pattern is confirmed on SciERC, where restricting to the favorable subset recovers a significant LP gain.
On Few-NERD, the trend is directionally consistent but the confidence interval crosses zero; the full-dataset result ($+1.39$~pp, $p{<}0.001$) reflects the larger sample size rather than a stronger per-instance effect.
CoNLL remains negative even on the favorable subset, consistent with the ceiling-regime interpretation: at $>$90\% greedy F1, residual errors are idiosyncratic and LP cannot rank corrections.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Implications.}
All signals achieve positive quality estimation across non-collapsed datasets, with rankings stable across model families and a 4B ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}; RE in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
For selection, LP tends to achieve gains when both factors are present (Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}); structural signals uniformly degrade selection.
The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal; effective selection likely requires content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}.

\paragraph{Why the gap exists.}
Two mechanisms block selection: \textit{instance degeneracy} (consensus-proximity) and \textit{weak LP-quality alignment} (per-sample).
Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility \cite{eikema2022sampling} correlates positively with F1 (SJ median $\rho{=}0.524$), but 17.8\% (SciERC) to 59.1\% (CoNLL) of instances produce identical F1 across all samples, eliminating headroom entirely (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
LP is severely compressed (median range 0.041 nats; Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}), with within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ ranging from 0.262 (SciERC) to 0.667 (Few-NERD; Table~\ref{tab:within_rho}).
Where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), within-instance $\rho$ rises to 0.39 and LP selection yields $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}).
An oracle tiebreaker within VC-equivalent groups recovers $+7.9$~pp, confirming per-sample signal exists but current signals cannot extract it (Appendices~\ref{app:n_scaling}, \ref{app:verbalized_confidence}, \ref{app:vc_quartile}).
Hidden state probes confirm richer information exists (SciERC MLP $\rho{=}0.388$ vs.\ LP $0.283$, $+37$\%), but the correlation-selection gap persists (gap closure $-5.1$\% vs.\ $+4.8$\%; \S\ref{sec:hidden_probe}): the bottleneck is diminishing marginal returns on selection, not information loss.

\paragraph{LP compression mechanisms.}
Four non-mutually-exclusive mechanisms contribute (Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}); entity-token LP shows $4{\times}$ higher variance yet performs worse; compression operates at the representation level, not token aggregation (Appendix~\ref{app:lp_failure_stability}).

\paragraph{Regime boundaries.}
QE signals collapse at the low-resource boundary (WNUT-17, conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}) and LP degrades selection at the ceiling (CoNLL, degeneracy 59--89\%, $-0.85$~pp).
Temperature manipulation provides the primary evidence that both factors appear independently associated with selection success: at $T{=}1.2$, degeneracy drops to 12.5\% yet LP does not improve because alignment remains weak ($\rho{=}0.225$ vs.\ Few-NERD ${\sim}$0.5; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}); the SciERC epoch curve corroborates this (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc}).
Approximate boundaries from our data: degeneracy ${<}$15\% and $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1}) \gtrsim 0.3$; temperature and training convergence are controllable levers (Tables~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}), while calibration cannot improve selection (Appendix~\ref{app:calibration_baseline}).

\paragraph{Capability-diversity tension.}
Degeneracy rises with model scale (4B: 10.4\% vs.\ 8B: 17.8\%; Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}), training convergence (Few-NERD: 14\% at 3 epochs to 31\% at 5; Tables~\ref{tab:fewnerd}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}, \ref{tab:epoch_scierc}), and model family (LLaMA 89.2\% vs.\ Qwen 59.1\% on CoNLL; Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).
For structured IE, the same training progress that reduces error also reduces the output diversity on which selection depends \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, snell2025scaling}.
This pattern is observational and does not establish causality, but the consistency across independent axes suggests a systematic relationship: as models improve, the window for test-time selection narrows.

\paragraph{From diagnosis to selection.}
A degeneracy-aware LP strategy (DALS) that gates on within-instance LP range yields modest gains but cannot overcome weak alignment (Appendix~\ref{app:dals}).
Entity-level majority voting, where the merged output includes all entities present in ${\geq}N/2$ samples, yields $+0.76$~pp on SciERC (5.8\% gap recovery) but $-0.64$~pp on CoNLL and $-3.21$~pp on Few-NERD (Appendix~\ref{app:entity_merge}). On degenerate subsets, merge is uniformly negative across all three datasets; entity-level aggregation cannot bypass the diversity bottleneck.
Hidden state probes (\S\ref{sec:hidden_probe}) confirm richer information exists ($+37$\% correlation) yet the gap persists (gap closure $-5.1$\% vs.\ LP's $+4.8$\%), reinforcing the capability-diversity tension.
